los.text: Identify and access appropriate prescribing resources to support clinical decision making
los.html:
ResourceUse
BNF (online, app, print)Indications, doses, renal and hepatic adjustment, interactions (appendix), side effects
BNF for Children (BNFc)Weight- and age-based paediatric dosing
NICE guidelines / CKSWhich drug to choose for a condition
Local formulary / trust guidelinesPreferred drugs, antibiotic policy
Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA)Drug safety updates
PharmacistInteractions, complex dosing, formulations
SmPC (electronic medicines compendium)Full product information

los.text: Understand the principles of prescribing from a legal and clinical perspective.
los.html:
Legal
  • Only registered prescribers (doctors, some nurses and pharmacists) can prescribe prescription-only medicines (POMs)
  • Controlled drugs have extra legal requirements (Misuse of Drugs Regulations: dose, form, strength and total quantity in words and figures)
  • The prescriber is accountable for every prescription.
Clinical
  • Right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time
  • Check allergies, interactions, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, and the patient's wishes.
Prescription must include
Patient name, DOB/hospital number, weight if relevant
Drug name (generic, capitals), dose, route, frequency, start date
Prescriber signature, printed name, bleep/GMC number
Allergy status
  • GMC good practice: prescribe only when you have adequate knowledge of the patient's health and are satisfied the drug serves their needs.

los.text: Describe key visual signs and interpret their relevance to clinical diagnosis
los.html:
SignLook forSuggests
GeneralWell/unwell, distress, breathlessness, postureSeverity
ColourPallor, cyanosis (central/peripheral), jaundice, flushingAnaemia, hypoxia, liver disease
HandsClubbing, tar staining, tremor, palmar erythemaLung/heart disease, smoking, liver disease
BreathingRate, accessory muscles, pursed lipsRespiratory distress, COPD
Body habitusCachexia, obesityChronic disease, malignancy
SkinRashes, bruising, scars, oedemaSystemic disease, previous surgery
Around the bedOxygen, inhalers, walking aids, sputum pot, catheterContext

los.text: Demonstrate the correct use of palpation techniques to assess anatomical structures as part of a clinical examination
los.html:
BeforeIntroduce, consent, wash hands, expose appropriately, warm hands, ask about pain, watch the face.
TechniqueFlat of the hand and fingers, start away from any pain, systematic order (e.g. all nine regions of the abdomen).
UseWhat you assess
Masses and organsSize, shape, surface, consistency, tenderness, mobility, pulsatility
TendernessGuarding, rebound (peritonism)
Temperature, pulsesBack of the hand for temperature
Expansion and fremitusChest

los.text: Distinguish between light and deep palpation techniques and justify their appropriate use in different clinical scenarios.
los.html:
Light palpationDeep palpation
Pressure~1 cm, gentle~4–5 cm, firmer
PurposeTenderness, guarding, superficial masses; reassures the patientOrgans (liver, spleen, kidneys) and deep masses
OrderFirstAfter light palpation
Avoid deep ifSevere tenderness, peritonism, suspected AAA (gentle only)

los.text: Understand and perform the technique of percussion as part of a clinical examination
los.html:
• Technique: hyperextend the middle finger of your non-dominant hand and press it firmly on the skin (pleximeter)
    • strike its middle phalanx with the tip of the middle finger of the other hand (plexor) with a quick wrist flick, then lift off.
  • Compare side to side, from top to bottom (chest), and from resonant to dull (to find an edge, e.g. liver).

los.text: Identify and interpret different percussion sounds and their clinical significance as part of a clinical examination
Demonstrate appropriate use of a stethoscope for auscultation of heart, lungs, and other organs
los.html:
DiaphragmHigh-pitched sounds (normal heart sounds, breath sounds, aortic/mitral regurgitation). Bell: low-pitched sounds (mitral stenosis, S3, bruits), held lightly.
TechniqueWarm it, skin contact (not through clothes), quiet room, ask the patient to breathe through the mouth.
AreaListen for
Heart (aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, mitral areas)S1, S2, added sounds, murmurs (timing, radiation)
Lungs (front, sides, back; compare both sides)Vesicular vs bronchial breathing, crackles, wheeze, rub
AbdomenBowel sounds (absent, tinkling), bruits (renal, aortic)
CarotidsBruits

los.text: Apply the standard structure for medical history taking in patient consultations
los.html:
1. IntroductionWash hands, introduce yourself (name and role), confirm patient identity, gain consent, ensure privacy.
2Presenting complaint (open question).
3History of presenting complaint.
4Past medical history, drug history and allergies.
5Family history, social history.
6Systems review.
7ICE, then summarise, thank and close.
  • Common cold example: onset
    • nasal symptoms
    • sore throat
    • cough
    • fever
    • red flags (breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, symptoms over 3 weeks)
    • contacts
    • self-care and when to seek help.

los.text: Develop strategies to build rapport with patients, showing empathy and communication skills
los.html:
StrategyExample
Warm introductionEye contact, smile, name and role
Open questions and active listeningLet the patient talk without interrupting
Empathy"That sounds really worrying"
Non-verbalOpen posture, nodding, appropriate eye level
Reflecting and summarisingShows you've understood
Respect and dignityPrivacy, appropriate language, no jargon
Exploring ICEShows you care about their view

los.text: Demonstrate professional and patient-centered introductions in clinical settings
los.html:
"Hello, my name is…"Introduce yourself with your full name and role (e.g. "medical student").
Confirm identityFull name and date of birth.
ConsentExplain what the consultation involves and ask permission; offer a chaperone for intimate examinations.
Comfort and privacyCurtains, seated at the same level, ask how they'd like to be addressed.
Hand hygiene before and after.
